ACCOUNT AUDIT SUMMARY

You don't have a leads problem.
You have a signal problem.

Fix the tracking. Consolidate by intent. Then let smart bidding do what it's actually good at — in that order.

CORE DIAGNOSIS

Across 90 days of data the account shows 243 phone-call conversions at $171 cost per conversion — but zero form fills coming through Google's tracking, on a landing page that has a working form prominently placed at the top. The form either isn't firing as a conversion event, or it's been double-counted somewhere else. Google's algorithm has been learning on a partial, inflated signal for the entire history of the account.

Layered on top of that: four search campaigns are splitting the conversion volume so thin that only one (Filtration Search) clears the 30-conversions-per-30-days threshold smart bidding actually needs to learn. The other three sit between 16 and 28. Target CPA is turned on in one campaign that doesn't have enough data to support it. The structure is starving the algorithm of the signal it would need to bid intelligently.

Fix the tracking and consolidate by intent. The signal stops being noise. Smart bidding starts compounding. The cost per lead stops being a ceiling and becomes a target.

01

WHAT BROKE — TRACKING IS LEAKING THE SIGNAL

Form fills aren't being tracked from Google traffic

The Filtration Search campaign — which carries a significant share of the budget — sends users to a landing page with a prominent, working form. Across 90 days, Google Ads shows zero form-fill conversions from that campaign. Two possibilities, both bad: either no one is filling out the form (extremely unlikely given the page quality) or the form-fill conversion event isn't firing into Google. The likeliest cause is the latter.

Google is a compounding platform. Every conversion teaches the algorithm what kind of person to look for next — age, income bracket, intent signal, audience overlap. Missing form fills means missing the highest-intent slice of the audience, and Google is rebuilding the lookalike pool every day on incomplete data.

FIX: Audit the form's conversion event — page-load fire, GTM tag, GA4 event, whichever path is configured. Confirm submissions are reaching Google as a primary conversion. Ship this before any bidding or structural change.

Multiple phone-call conversion actions risk double-counting

The account currently has multiple phone-call conversion goals running in parallel. That can be intentional (different numbers on different page sections, or call extensions vs. website calls), but it can also silently double-count the same lead — once when the call extension fires and again when the website call event triggers. If Google sees inflated audience signal, it bids harder for the wrong people.

FIX: Map every phone-call conversion source. Confirm each call lead is counted exactly once. Set primary vs. secondary conversion flags so smart bidding optimizes against the unified, deduped count.

02

WHAT BROKE — TOO FRAGMENTED TO LEARN

Four search campaigns, only one clears the smart-bidding threshold

Smart bidding (Target CPA, Maximize Conversions with Target) needs roughly 30 conversions per campaign per 30 days to learn consistently. Across the four enabled search campaigns, the 30-day numbers look like this: Filtration Search at 32 (clears it), the others at 28, 27, 26, 16. Three out of four are sitting just below or well below the threshold.

The Filtration Search campaign is currently using Target CPA — which is the right intent — but it doesn't have enough conversion volume yet to bid against that target consistently. The bid strategy will keep oscillating, costing efficiency.

FIX: Consolidate to two search campaigns split by intent (next page). That concentrates the signal and gets each campaign over the smart-bidding threshold.

Service-level segmentation isn't earning its keep

The current campaigns are split by service (filtration, water bans, etc.). The reason to give different services their own campaigns is to control budget independently, set different CPA targets, or target different geographies. None of those are happening here — every campaign has the same daily budget, the same service area, and (mostly) Maximize Conversions bidding. The split is creating fragmentation cost without producing any of the benefits it would normally justify.

FIX: Move services down a level into ad groups inside two consolidated campaigns. Service-level control comes back through ad-group-level CPA targets when volume justifies it.

03

THE STRUCTURE — SPLIT BY INTENT, NOT BY SERVICE

The right way to segment a lead-gen account at this volume is by buyer intent — what stage the searcher is in — not by which product line they typed.

Two campaigns. One funnel.

  • High-intent search — every keyword that includes "near me" or a specific city name. These are people closer to picking up the phone than picking up an article. They convert at materially higher rates.
  • Research search — broader informational queries: "what is a water filtration system," "how does a well pump work," "best filtration company [region]." These convert later (or never), but they teach the audience and they show up again on a high-intent search a week later when remembering the brand matters.

Budget split: 70 / 30

Roughly 70% of the daily budget into the high-intent campaign, 30% into research. Both campaigns now compound the signal Google needs. The high-intent one will hit the smart-bidding threshold first; research follows once the audience pool builds up.

Once the structure is right, the algorithm has enough volume in each campaign to learn from. The CPA in the high-intent campaign drops first. The research campaign keeps brand awareness flowing into future high-intent searches. The funnel starts compounding.

FIX — important: Do this slowly. Move keywords in small batches (a few per week), check performance, and only proceed when the account is stable. Big restructures throw Google into a learning phase that can take months to recover from. The plan is right, but the rollout has to be patient.

04

WHAT'S WORKING — THE LANDING PAGE IS RARE

Most accounts at this spend level have a half-broken landing page somewhere in the funnel. Clear Water Pump's filtration landing page is genuinely well-built, and that's worth saying explicitly:

  • The form is open and prominent — top of the page, immediately scannable, low friction.
  • Below the fold: real social proof — 15+ years in business, A+ rated, customer reviews — exactly where it should be.
  • The layout itself is uncommonly well-organized for a service-business landing page.

One gap: the page is missing visual content

The upper section needs an image carousel or short video, equal in width to the form, showing real installation work — technicians at customer homes, the actual filtration equipment, people doing the job. Organic, human, and specific to the work — not stock photography.

Service-business buyers convert when they feel comfortable. Visual content of the actual work is the cheapest way to manufacture that comfort. Quality Score gets a small lift; conversion rate gets a bigger one.

FIX: Add a 3–5-image carousel or a 30-second installation video to the upper half of the landing page, equal width to the form. Outside the ad-account scope — Clear Water Pump's web team executes; Grow My Ads can spec the placement and dimensions.

05

DEFINING A PROFITABLE CPA

The current $171 cost-per-conversion number is misleading on its own. Two adjustments are needed before it becomes a useful planning number:

Not every Google "conversion" closes on the back end

Of those 243 phone-call conversions over 90 days, only a fraction become paying customers. Service-business close rates typically land somewhere between 30% and 50%. So the effective cost per closed customer is somewhere closer to $340–$570, not $171.

The right CPA target depends on numbers Grow My Ads doesn't have yet

To set a Target CPA that actually drives profit, three pieces of information are needed:

  • Average order value — what's a typical job worth?
  • Lifetime value — does the customer come back for service, repairs, upgrades, replacement?
  • Close rate — what percent of leads from Google convert into paying jobs?

Once those numbers are in hand, the CPA target maths out cleanly. Realistic post-rebuild range: $80–$110 per conversion with cleaner tracking and a consolidated structure. Not $20 — but materially below the current $171.

FIX: Provide AOV, LTV, and close rate (or estimates) so Grow My Ads can calculate the actual profitable CPA target before any bidding changes are made.

PRIORITY STACK — DO IT IN THIS ORDER

Scope: Grow My Ads executes the Google Ads work directly. Form-fill tracking on the website may need Clear Water Pump's web team to add or fix the tag/event firing. Visual content on the landing page is a Clear Water Pump web-team task. That makes Clear Water Pump the bottleneck on items 02 and 03.
  1. 01

    Audit and rebuild conversion tracking Grow My Ads

    Map every conversion source, dedupe phone calls, confirm form-fill firing, set primary vs. secondary flags. Nothing else moves until tracking is clean.

  2. 02

    Fix form-fill conversion event firing Joint

    If the issue is a missing tag on the page, Clear Water Pump's web team installs it; Grow My Ads configures the Ads-side import and primary-conversion flag.

  3. 03

    Add image carousel or video to the landing page Clear Water Pump / web team

    Upper half of the page, equal width to the form. Real installation work, not stock. Outside the ad-account scope; Grow My Ads specs.

  4. 04

    Confirm AOV, LTV, and close rate Joint

    Numbers from Clear Water Pump; Grow My Ads converts them into a Target CPA that actually drives profit.

  5. 05

    Consolidate to two intent-based campaigns — slowly Grow My Ads

    Move keywords in small weekly batches. High-intent (near me / city) and Research are the two destination campaigns. Services live as ad groups.

  6. 06

    Move bidding to TCPA once campaigns clear 30 conv / 30 days Grow My Ads

    High-intent campaign hits the threshold first. Research follows. PMax can re-enter at a tighter CPA underneath once the search side is stable.

  7. 07

    Layer remarketing and YouTube on top of warm traffic Grow My Ads

    High-intent service clicks are expensive — most don't convert on the first visit. Amplify them.

07

EXPECTATION SETTING — THIS IS A 90-DAY REBUILD

MONTH 1

Tracking rebuild. First wave of consolidation — small keyword batches moved weekly. CPA may rise briefly while the cleaner conversion signal lands.

MONTH 2

High-intent campaign clears the 30-conversion threshold. Bid strategy migrates to Target CPA. Research campaign keeps building audience pool.

MONTH 3

Research campaign joins the smart-bidding tier. Cost per closed customer stabilizes downward. Remarketing and YouTube layered on warm traffic.

AFTER

Push spend on the campaigns hitting their CPA target. OCT pipeline data feeds bids — Google bids harder for the leads that actually become paying jobs.

What Grow My Ads doesn't promise: any improvement in week 1. The consolidation has to be done in chunks of a few keywords per week, not all at once. Big swings throw Google's algorithm into a learning phase that can take 60–90 days to recover from. The playbook is sound; the rest is the discipline to wait.

Visual content on the landing page is on Clear Water Pump's side — and it affects Quality Score and conversion rate regardless of how the ad account is structured.
